analysis.one_liner: Bans hydraulic fracturing on federally owned land leased for oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban fracking on leased federal land was introduced in December 2014 with one cosponsor and died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the law governing federal mineral leases so that no company could use hydraulic fracturing — fracking — on land owned by the United States and leased to private drillers. It would only apply to new leases or leases being renewed, so companies with existing leases could keep drilling as they are until those leases came up for renewal. The bill was introduced in the last month of a two-year Congress, never got a hearing, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or use federal public lands — for drinking water, recreation, or simply as shared public property — would gain protection from the water use, chemical use, and possible groundwater and air contamination associated with fracking. Taxpayers who own the land jointly would see their property protected from intensive industrial drilling activity.

how_it_helps.text: It would bar any activity under a federal mineral lease conducted for the purpose of hydraulic fracturing, keeping fracking off land owned by the public.
It defines fracking broadly to cover operations that fracture reservoir rock to increase hydrocarbon flow, while leaving conventional water flooding and other secondary recovery methods allowed.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to fracking on new and renewed federal leases, and the royalties and energy production from public lands would decline. Some rural communities that host drilling and collect related revenue would forgo that economic activity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers on federal land

drawbacks.text: The ban would only apply when a lease is renewed or adjusted, so fracking on leases already in effect could continue — the bill would not stop current drilling, only prevent it in the future.
Blocking fracking on federal land would reduce domestic oil and gas production and the federal royalties from public-land drilling, a cost supporters of energy production would point to.
The definition excludes conventional secondary and tertiary recovery methods, so some well-stimulation activity that critics might consider similar to fracking would still be permitted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — protecting water, air, and publicly owned land from fracking on federal leases — was real but prospective only: the grandfather clause meant existing leases could continue until renewed, so the bill would have phased in slowly. The cost, acknowledged by supporters of drilling, would have fallen on oil and gas production and the royalties federal leasing generates, some of which funds state and federal programs. The bigger design problem was timing: it was introduced in the last weeks of a Congress with essentially no support, so it was never seriously weighed at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the Congress, referred to the Natural Resources Committee and then to an energy subcommittee, and the Congress ended before anyone ever acted on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 10, 2014, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
Twelve days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it sat.
It never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies with federal leases are better off: fracking on public land remains fully permitted, including under leases that would have been covered once renewed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land

for.name: Rep. Mark Pocan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban fracking on leased federal land.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Doc Hastings (R-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; both sponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported it, but with only two backers the bill never rose to a real partisan test.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies seeking new federal leases
industries.note: The bill would make it impossible to frack any new or renewed federal lease, cutting off a large source of drilling opportunities on public land. If it had passed, companies would have had to rely on private and state lands for new fracking wells.

industries.industry: Holders of existing federal oil and gas leases
industries.note: Because the ban applies only upon renewal or readjustment of a lease, companies already holding federal leases could keep fracking them, effectively locking in their position while closing the door to new entrants.
